traveler: Fernão de Magalhães (Ferdinand Magellan, Hernando de Magallanes)
title: The Passage and the Shallow Water: Magellan from the Malabar Coast to Mactan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Porto, the birth without a document
stops.date_confidence: unattested. No register names the day, the month, or the town. Four candidates compete: Sabrosa, Porto, Vila Nova de Gaia, Ponte da Barca. Modern Portuguese scholarship (Torre do Tombo materials, the Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion, José Manuel Garcia) leans to Porto, reported here at second hand and not checked against the archive. Date defaulted to 1480-01-01 from the conventional c. 1480.
stops.campa: No parish register names the day. Four towns in the north of Portugal keep a claim on him, Sabrosa, Porto, Vila Nova de Gaia, Ponte da Barca, and the archives settle none of them. Modern Portuguese scholarship leans to Porto, the granite city at the mouth of the Douro, where the hulls that go to Africa are laid down and the ropewalks run along the river. A boy is born there, or near there, around 1480, into the lesser nobility of a kingdom that has staked its whole treasury on the sea. Almost everything after this is documented. This is not.
suggested_refs: The Torre do Tombo materials on the Magalhães family, on which the Porto attribution rests

stops.name: Sabrosa, the house of Pereira
stops.date_confidence: the claim is a documented forgery, not an attested birth. Wikipedia, 'Sabrosa': the Sabrosa birthplace documents were manufactured in the eighteenth century by António Luís Álvares Pereira Coelho da Silva Castelo-Branco e Magalhães (1751-1802) to present himself as Magellan's heir. Date is an ordering device only, one day after the Porto stop. Coordinates 41.2844, -7.5950 per the Sabrosa article; a variant 41.2667, -7.5667 in circulation is about two kilometres off and is not used here.
stops.campa: Inland, in the wine country above the Douro, Sabrosa shows the Solar dos Magalhães and says the navigator was born under its roof. The documents that prove it were manufactured in the eighteenth century by a local nobleman who wanted a great man for an ancestor and wrote himself one. The forgery has been known for a long time and the town keeps the claim regardless. A statue of Magellan stands in the square, and the town holds civic ties with Cebu City and with Puerto San Julián.
suggested_refs: The Solar dos Magalhães (House of Pereira) at Sabrosa and the town's Magellan statue

stops.name: Lisbon, the household of Queen Leonor
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The placement of the boy in Queen Leonor's household from about age twelve, and his passage into crown service in 1495 under Manuel I, come from the standard biographical tradition; the 1492 date is reported by the Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion at second hand and was not independently confirmed. No document from these years survives. Court coordinates are Lisbon generally; no specific palace is identified in the sources checked.
stops.campa: At about twelve he is placed as a page in the household of Queen Leonor, and he learns what such boys learn: cartography, celestial navigation, the handling of a horse, the etiquette of a court that is spending everything it has on the road to India. In 1495 Manuel I comes to the throne and the boy passes into royal service under a king who will never much like him. Not a schoolbook survives, not a payment order, nothing. The education is inferred backward from the man who will later read a chart and argue with cosmographers about it.
suggested_refs: Portuguese royal household records of Queen Leonor's court, in which no entry for Magellan has been located

stops.name: Restelo, the armada of Dom Francisco de Almeida
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sailing (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). Coordinates are the Belém waterfront generally: the Tower postdates 1505 and stands here as a landmark proxy, not as the structure he sailed from.
stops.campa: The fleet of Dom Francisco de Almeida, first viceroy of Portuguese India, stands out from the Lisbon waterfront, and Fernão de Magalhães, about twenty-five, is aboard one of the ships as a supernumerary gentleman soldier. He will not see Portugal again for seven years. The armada carries orders to build forts down the East African and Indian coasts and to shut the Red Sea route to the spice trade at its source. He goes out an unknown volunteer in the largest fleet his kingdom has ever sent east.
suggested_refs: The 1505 armada of the first viceroy, twenty-two ships, largest Portuguese fleet sent to the Indian Ocean

stops.name: Cannanore, the wound at the fort
stops.date_confidence: attested that he fought and was wounded at Cannanore in 1506 (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Kannur Fort'). The month is an approximation within the 1506 siege season; the detail descends through the Portuguese chroniclers, Gaspar Correia among them, not through any log in his own hand.
stops.campa: Almeida raised a fort at Cannanore the previous October, and the Zamorin's coalition comes against it with an army on the land side and a fleet on the water. Magellan is inside the fighting and is wounded there. It is the first blood he loses in the East and the first of the woundings that will accumulate on him across sixteen years, leg, arm, face, ending on a beach in the Visayas. What is known of it reaches us through the chroniclers of the Portuguese in Asia, who were writing decades later and had reasons of their own.
suggested_refs: Fort St Angelo at Kannur, raised by Almeida in October 1505

stops.name: Fort Kochi, the garrison years
stops.date_confidence: inferred for the date, attested for the service. Magellan's Malabar posting across roughly 1505-1512 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Fort Emmanuel'); the 1507 pin is a mid-span placeholder for years with no dated events attached to him. Research notes also place him at Quilon/Kollam in these years, which could not be confirmed against a landmark source.
stops.campa: Cochin is the Portuguese base on the Malabar coast, and Fort Emmanuel, raised for Manuel I in 1503, is the first European fortress in Asia. Magellan is in and out of it for years, on the coastal patrols, the convoy escorts, the burnings of Muslim shipping that keep the pepper route Portuguese. He holds no title and no command in these years. What he takes out of them is the monsoon: when it turns, how far a hull can be pushed against it, and in what season a coast can be worked at all.
suggested_refs: Fort Emmanuel at Fort Kochi, first European fort built in Asia

stops.name: Diu, the fleet that broke the coalition
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested; Magellan's personal presence is not. The Battle of Diu, 3 February 1509, is beyond dispute. That Magellan was in the fleet rests on chronicle tradition and on every subsequent biographer, and no document from the day names him. Recorded here as a stop the record cannot close.
stops.campa: Almeida brings the Portuguese fleet against a combined Mamluk, Gujarati and Calicut force in the roadstead off Diu and destroys it. After Diu no other navy contests the western Indian Ocean for the rest of the century, and the spice route belongs to Lisbon by force of gunnery. Magellan is placed in this fleet by the chronicle tradition and by every biographer who has written about him. No document from the day names him. He was almost certainly there and it cannot be proved.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Diu, 3 February 1509, and Diu Fort
sources: General historiography of the Battle of Diu (not independently re-fetched)

stops.name: Malacca, the ambush and Francisco Serrão
stops.date_confidence: attested for the expedition and its collapse (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'); month is approximate within 1509. The account that Magellan personally went back for Serrão is biographical tradition rather than document, and is given here as such.
stops.campa: Diogo Lopes de Sequeira takes four ships to Malacca to open trade, and Magellan sails with him. Alongside him is Francisco Serrão, his friend and probably his kinsman. The sultan's men lay an ambush; the Portuguese ashore are attacked, the ships are nearly taken, and the expedition retreats with its dead. Magellan is among those who get out, and by one account he goes back into the boats to pull Serrão out of it. Serrão will end his life in the Moluccas, and the letters he sends from there to Magellan describe islands where the clove grows wild.
suggested_refs: The letters of Francisco Serrão from Ternate to Magellan, now lost, known only by report

stops.name: Old Goa, the council of Albuquerque
stops.date_confidence: reported, not independently verified. The October 1510 council and Magellan's presence in it derive from the Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion as reported within a research dossier; the specific council date could not be confirmed against a fetched source. The November recapture of Goa itself is standard and attested (Wikipedia, 'Old Goa').
stops.campa: Afonso de Albuquerque has taken Goa in the spring and lost it again by summer, and in October he calls a council of his captains on whether to try a second time. Magellan sits in it. He is nobody's admiral and holds no command, and he is consulted anyway: after five years in the East his opinion on an amphibious assault is worth having in the room. In November the city is stormed and held, and Goa becomes the capital of Portuguese Asia for four hundred and fifty years.
suggested_refs: Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion, entry on Magellan's Indian service, for the October 1510 council
sources: Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion (reported at second hand, unverified)

stops.name: Malacca, the conquest and the man called Enrique
stops.date_confidence: attested that Magellan took part in Albuquerque's 1511 conquest and that he acquired the enslaved man later called Enrique in Malacca or its region that year (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'A Famosa'). The precise day of the acquisition is unrecorded; the date given is the fall of the city.
stops.campa: Albuquerque comes back to Malacca in force and takes the city, the entrepot where the Indian Ocean trade, the China trade and the spice islands all meet. Here, or somewhere in these months, Magellan acquires an enslaved man from the region and has him baptised Enrique, who will serve him as interpreter for the next ten years and outlive him. The fortress A Famosa goes up on the hill afterward, built in part out of the rubble of the mosques and the tombs the Portuguese pulled down.
suggested_refs: A Famosa and St Paul's Hill, Malacca, raised after the 1511 conquest

segments.name: The King Who Would Not Have Him

stops.name: Lisbon, the return with Enrique
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1512 return from Asia with Enrique (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'); month defaulted within the year, no day recorded.
stops.campa: He comes home after seven years with a small pension, an enslaved interpreter, and no particular standing. Men who went out with him and stayed now hold governorships; Serrão has a house and a wife in Ternate and a position at a sultan's court. Magellan has letters from the Moluccas and a conviction he cannot finance: that the spice islands lie so far east that under the line drawn at Tordesillas they may fall on Castile's side of the world, and that a passage west to them exists. He is thirty-two, and at the Portuguese court nobody is listening.
stops.quote: Ferdinand Magellan, a distinguished Portuguese, who, for many years had explored the coasts of the whole of the East as Admiral
stops.quote_source: Maximilianus Transylvanus, Letter to the Cardinal of Salzburg (De Moluccis Insulis, 1523), English translation in The First Voyage Round the World
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Tordesillas line of 1494 and the unresolved antimeridian question in the Moluccas

stops.name: Azemmour, the leg and the horse
stops.date_confidence: contradiction between sources, not resolved. Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan' has him sustain a leg wound in August 1513 that left a permanent limp. Wikipedia, 'Azemmour' says only that he lost his horse in skirmishes outside the city. Both are carried; neither is silently adopted. The city fell on 1 September 1513.
stops.campa: Portugal throws an army against Azemmour on the Moroccan coast, and the city falls on the first of September with almost no resistance offered. Magellan is in the skirmishing outside the walls. The biographical tradition says he took a lance wound in the leg there and was lame for the rest of his life. The Portuguese account of the campaign says only that he lost his horse. Both statements survive, they do not agree, and the limp that everyone in Seville describes four years later has to have come from somewhere.
suggested_refs: The 1513 Portuguese campaign against Azemmour under James, Duke of Braganza

stops.name: Lisbon, no further offers
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction. Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan' gives 15 May 1514 as the date from which Magellan received no further offers of employment from the crown. Research notes had inverted this into the receipt of a last offer, which also contradicted the 1515 crewman's berth he is recorded as refusing. The end-of-offers reading is the one used here.
stops.campa: The record marks the fifteenth of May 1514 as the end of it. From that day the crown makes him no further offer of employment, and a man who has spent eight years in Asia and one summer in Morocco is left standing in Lisbon with a pension he could live on and nothing to do. In 1515 a place is put in front of him, a crewman's berth on another man's ship, and he refuses it. The man who sat in Albuquerque's council of war before Goa is being told that he may serve before the mast or not at all.
suggested_refs: Portuguese crown employment records after 15 May 1514, in which Magellan does not appear

stops.name: Lisbon, the renunciation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1517 as the year of the final quarrel with Manuel I, the renunciation of Portuguese nationality, and the departure for Castile (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). No month or day is recorded; defaulted to January. The content of the final audience is traditional.
stops.campa: He asks Manuel I one last time and is refused one last time, and by the standard account he asks whether he may then offer his service elsewhere, and the king tells him he may go where he pleases. He goes. He renounces his Portuguese nationality, which in 1517 is not a formality but a legal act with consequences reaching his family, and crosses into Castile. Portuguese pilots who take service with Spain are counted traitors in Lisbon and are hunted for it, bribed back, sometimes killed. He makes the crossing anyway.
suggested_refs: Portuguese diplomatic correspondence on pilots who defected to Castile, 1517-1519

segments.name: Seville, the Gate of the Indies

stops.name: Seville, the Casa de la Contratación
stops.date_confidence: attested for the October 1517 arrival in Seville (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'); day defaulted within the month. The specific housing of the Casa de la Contratación inside the Real Alcázar in this exact period was not re-verified against a fetched source, and the network of Barbosa, Aranda, Fonseca and Haro is reported here from a research dossier rather than from primary record.
stops.campa: Seville in October, and the whole American trade of Castile runs through one building: the Casa de la Contratación, which licenses every ship, holds every chart, and examines every pilot before he is allowed to sail. Magellan walks into a city thick with Portuguese who have made the same crossing he has. Diogo Barbosa, once of Lisbon, is alcaide of the arsenal. Juan de Aranda is a factor of the Casa. Behind them stand Bishop Fonseca, who runs the Indies for the crown, and Cristóbal de Haro, who has the money.
suggested_refs: The Casa de la Contratación archive, Seville, and the padrón real of licensed charts
sources: Research dossier account of the Seville network (unverified against primary record)

stops.name: Seville, the marriage to Beatriz Barbosa
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Wikipedia places the marriage in 1517; History.com places it within a year of the October arrival. No month or day located, defaulted to December. Coordinates are the atlas's standing Seville pin (37.3891, -5.9945), inherited for cartographic consistency; no church or house is identified in the sources.
stops.campa: He marries Beatriz Barbosa, Diogo's daughter, and takes a dowry and a family with her. The marriage does what marriages do in a merchant city: it makes the foreigner local, and it makes his enterprise a family enterprise. Her kinsman Duarte Barbosa, who has been to India himself and written a book about what he saw there, joins the expedition and becomes one of Magellan's lieutenants. A son, Rodrigo, is born the next year in this city. Duarte Barbosa will be killed at a banquet in Cebu four days after Magellan dies.
suggested_refs: Duarte Barbosa, Livro do que viu e ouviu no Oriente, written c. 1516

stops.name: Valladolid, the capitulaciones
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Capitulaciones de Valladolid, 22 March 1518, and for the Order of Santiago commandership (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Corrected against research notes: the contract title is capitán general, not admiral. Coordinates are standard Valladolid city geography, not a verified building.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of March the eighteen-year-old Charles I signs the capitulaciones with Magellan and the cosmographer Ruy Faleiro. They are to reach the Moluccas sailing west, inside Castile's half of the world, which is what Columbus promised this same crown and did not deliver. They are granted a twentieth of the profits, governorship of whatever they find, and five ships. Magellan's commission reads capitán general, not admiral, a distinction his Castilian officers will make a great deal of before the year 1520 is out. Charles also makes him a Commander of the Order of Santiago.
suggested_refs: The Capitulaciones de Valladolid, 22 March 1518, inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2023
sources: UNESCO Memory of the World register, 2023 inscription

stops.name: Seville, the fleet goes down the river
stops.date_confidence: attested. 10 August 1519 is the departure from Seville down the Guadalquivir, not from Sanlúcar; research notes had welded the Seville date to the Sanlúcar place. Crew of roughly 270 confirmed (History.com; Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Coordinates are the Torre del Oro, the traditional river mooring, offered as a landmark proxy rather than a documented berth.
stops.campa: Five ships warp off the Seville quay on the tenth of August and drop down the Guadalquivir toward the sea: Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria, Santiago. Aboard are roughly two hundred and seventy men, Castilians, Portuguese, Genoese, Greeks, Flemings, and a Venetian gentleman named Antonio Pigafetta who has attached himself to the voyage in order to see things and write them down. His is the fullest account of the voyage that survives. The fleet anchors at Sanlúcar and lies there more than five weeks over its stores and its orders.
suggested_refs: The Torre del Oro on the Guadalquivir, traditional mooring of the Indies fleets

stops.name: Seville, the will
stops.date_confidence: attested for the will of 24 August 1519 and its provisions (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). The quoted burial clause is given here from Ambeth Ocampo's newspaper translation; the original Spanish archival text was not located or fetched, so the exact wording is secondhand.
stops.campa: Two weeks before he sails he sets his affairs down in writing. Provision for Beatriz and for the boy Rodrigo; an entailed inheritance; masses to be said for his soul on the day of his burial; a legacy to his page Cristóbal Rebelo; and the freedom of Enrique of Malacca, effective at his own death, with money to go with it. The clause freeing Enrique will be ignored by every man who survives him. The last provision names the ground he wants to be buried in, and allows for the case in which he dies at sea.
stops.quote: if he dies in Seville, that he be buried in the Monastery of Santa Maria de la Victoria in Triana; but if he dies during his voyage, that he be buried in a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary closest to the spot where he died.
stops.quote_source: Magellan's testament, 24 August 1519, translated in Ambeth Ocampo, 'Magellan's last will and testament,' Philippine Daily Inquirer
suggested_refs: Magellan's testament of 24 August 1519, Seville, and the Monastery of Santa María de la Victoria at Triana
sources: Ambeth Ocampo, 'Magellan's last will and testament,' Philippine Daily Inquirer

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, standing out to sea
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Sanlúcar de Barrameda'; Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Sanlúcar pin on pedro_de_mendoza.journey.json, whose own file names Magellan at this port. The sailing orders described are standard fleet practice of the voyage as reported; the secrecy of the route is traditional characterization.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of September the five ships clear the bar at the mouth of the Guadalquivir and turn southwest into the Atlantic. The crews have confessed and taken communion. The sailing orders require every ship to salute the flagship at dusk and hold her lantern in sight through the night. Magellan does not tell his captains where he intends to go. Three of them are Castilian gentlemen appointed by the crown to keep watch on a Portuguese, and they suspect already that the route in his head is not the route written into the contract.
stops.quote: Magellan, who had already made up his mind either to die or to complete his enterprise
stops.quote_source: Maximilianus Transylvanus, Letter to the Cardinal of Salzburg (1523), translated in The First Voyage Round the World
suggested_refs: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, port of departure and of return for the circumnavigation

segments.name: The Atlantic and the Coast of Giants

stops.name: Tenerife, the last water under a Christian crown
stops.date_confidence: reported, not independently verified. The Canaries call is given in the research dossier and is standard in accounts of the voyage, but was not confirmed against a fetched source; the day is an estimate from the 20 September departure. The atlas holds a Canaries pin at La Gomera (28.0916, -17.1115) on columbus.journey.json; it is a different island and is not inherited here. The Cartagena quarrel over the course change is traditional.
stops.campa: Magellan turns south along the African coast instead of west across the ocean, and Juan de Cartagena, who commands the San Antonio and was put aboard by the crown to watch him, demands to know by what authority the course has been altered. The captain general answers that the captains are to follow his flag and to ask nothing further. Nine months later Cartagena will be put ashore on a Patagonian beach with a priest. Before any of that, the fleet lies in the Canaries taking on wood, water, pitch and fresh provisions, the last of any of it under a Christian crown.
suggested_refs: The Canary Islands as the standing Atlantic watering station of Iberian fleets
sources: Research dossier account of the Canaries call (unverified)

stops.name: Cabo de Santo Agostinho, the first American landfall
stops.date_confidence: attested for a late November 1519 landfall near Cabo de Santo Agostinho (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'); the exact day is not fixed in the source and 29 November is the conventional figure.
stops.campa: After weeks in the equatorial calms, with the pitch running out of the seams and the sharks keeping company under the counter, land comes up near the cape the Portuguese call Santo Agostinho. It is Brazil, and Brazil is Portuguese, which is precisely why Magellan does not stop there. He runs south along a coast he knows better than any Castilian aboard, past the Portuguese trading posts and their agents, looking for empty water in which to rest a fleet that flies the wrong flag.
suggested_refs: Cabo de Santo Agostinho, Pernambuco, southern limit of the earliest Portuguese Brazil

stops.name: Guanabara Bay, a fortnight ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the December 1519 stay at Guanabara Bay and for the execution of Antonio Salamón on 20 December 1519 (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Research notes had dated the garroting to January 1520, which is impossible: the fleet left the bay on 27 December 1519. Corrected here.
stops.campa: They come into the great bay on the thirteenth of December and stay a fortnight. The people of the shore bring fish, pineapples, sweet potatoes, and take playing cards, fishhooks, small bells in exchange. Pigafetta writes down everything he is shown and a good deal he is not: the hammocks, the canoes cut from single trunks, the eating of enemies, the sexual arrangements of a place he has no words for. On the twentieth of December Antonio Salamón, master of the Victoria, is garroted on that beach after conviction for rape. On the twenty-seventh the fleet weighs.
suggested_refs: Pigafetta's Brazilian ethnography, the longest continuous descriptive passage of the voyage's first year

stops.name: Río de la Plata, the false strait
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sighting on 11 January 1520 and exploration running into February (Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Research notes had dated the whole episode to February; corrected. Coordinates are an approximate estuary entrance, not a specific landmark. The Solís detail is standard background and was not re-verified.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of January an opening comes up in the coast so wide that the far shore cannot be seen from the deck, and the water at its mouth is still salt. Juan Díaz de Solís found this place four years ago and was killed on its bank. Magellan works the boats up it for weeks, sounding, tasting, watching the lead come up soft, and the water turns fresh under them. It is a river. He goes back out and turns south again, into latitudes no European chart describes, with the southern summer already past its height.
suggested_refs: The 1516 expedition of Juan Díaz de Solís to the Río de la Plata
sources: Research dossier account of the estuary survey

stops.name: Puerto San Julián, the winter camp
stops.date_confidence: attested for the wintering, 31 March to 21 August 1520 (Wikipedia, 'Puerto San Julián'). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Puerto San Julián pin on saint_erasmus.journey.json (-49.3, -67.72); geographic sources give -49.3, -67.7167. The Patagoni naming and the seizure of two men are from Pigafetta by way of the standard accounts.
stops.campa: On the last day of March, with the days shortening and the land going to gravel and wind, Magellan puts the fleet into a bare harbour at forty-nine degrees south and cuts the rations. They will be here five months. The coast looks empty until it is not: very tall men in guanaco skins come down to the water, and Pigafetta, struck by the size of their hide boots, calls them Patagoni. The name attaches itself to the whole country and has never come off. Magellan has two of them chained and shipped as a present for the king of Spain. Neither survives the voyage.
suggested_refs: Puerto San Julián, wintering anchorage of the fleet, 31 March to 21 August 1520

stops.name: Puerto San Julián, the mutiny at Easter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Easter mutiny of Cartagena, Quesada and Mendoza, the killing of Mendoza by Gonzalo Gómez de Espinosa, the execution of Quesada and the later marooning of Cartagena (Wikipedia, 'Puerto San Julián'; Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). Contemporary testimony is partisan on both sides and the legality of the proceedings was contested by Magellan's opponents; that dispute is not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: On Easter night Cartagena, Quesada and Mendoza take three of the five ships. They want the fleet turned for home, or at least turned east for the Cape of Good Hope, and they hold the Castilian half of it. Magellan sends a boat across to the Victoria with six armed men and a letter, and Mendoza is reading the letter when Gonzalo Gómez de Espinosa puts a knife into his throat. By morning the harbour mouth is blocked and the mutineers have nowhere to go. Quesada is beheaded. Cartagena is put ashore months later with a priest and left there.
suggested_refs: The gallows at Puerto San Julián, whose remains Francis Drake's crew reported finding in 1578

stops.name: Puerto San Julián, the lights on the mastheads
stops.date_confidence: placeholder, heavily hedged, and inherited as such. Pigafetta records the corpo santo but gives neither date nor position within the 1519-1522 voyage. The atlas already pins the sighting to Puerto San Julián on saint_erasmus.journey.json at -49.3, -67.72, that file having moved it off an internally impossible original pin at the Strait's Atlantic mouth. The same pin and the same reasoning are used here; the day is arbitrary within the wintering.
stops.campa: In a storm on this coast the crews see fire standing on the mastheads, a pale flame that does not burn the wood it stands on. The Portuguese call it corpo santo, the body of the saint, and take it for Saint Erasmus keeping watch over the ship, and a man who sees it is told he will not drown that night. Pigafetta writes the sighting into his journal and gives it neither a date nor a position, so it is set here, in the wintering anchorage, for want of anywhere better to put it. What the crews made of it, after the beheading on the beach, the journal does not say.
suggested_refs: Pigafetta's record of the corpo santo, and the sailors' cult of Saint Erasmus in the Iberian fleets
sources: working/journeys/saint_erasmus.journey.json, stop 'Puerto San Julian, the lights on the mastheads'

stops.name: Santa Cruz river, the loss of the Santiago
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Santiago was wrecked in a storm in May 1520 while surveying south of San Julián, with the crew surviving (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). The exact day is not fixed. Coordinates are an approximation from general Patagonian coastal geography: an attempted fetch of a page confirming the exact wreck site returned a 404, and the pin is not a verified landmark.
stops.campa: Magellan sends the smallest ship, the Santiago, south under João Serrão to scout the coast. She is caught by a squall at a river mouth and driven ashore and broken up. Every man aboard gets off except one, and the fleet is four ships from that day. Which river mouth it was no account fixes; it is somewhere south of San Julián. The survivors walk back north up the Patagonian coast in winter, eating shellfish, and the two who go ahead for help arrive so far gone that nobody recognises them.
suggested_refs: The Santa Cruz river mouth, approximate wreck site of the Santiago
sources: Research dossier account of the Santiago wreck (site unverified)

segments.name: The Strait and the Peaceful Sea

stops.name: Cabo Vírgenes, the opening
stops.date_confidence: attested for 21 October 1520 as the date the fleet reached the Atlantic entrance (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; History.com). Cabo Vírgenes as the specific eastern entrance point is standard geography and was not confirmed by a landmark-level fetch. The reconnaissance detail is from the standard accounts.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of October, the feast of Saint Ursula and the eleven thousand virgins, a headland comes up with a bay running west behind it. Every bay on this coast for eight months has turned out to be a bay. The pilots want to go on south. Magellan sends the San Antonio and the Concepción in to look, gives them five days, and waits at the mouth. When the two ships come back they come back firing their guns and flying every flag aboard, and the water they have sounded is salt the whole way in.
stops.quote: it issues in another sea, which is called the peaceful sea
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: Cabo Vírgenes, eastern entrance of the Strait of Magellan

stops.name: The strait, the naming of All Saints
stops.date_confidence: attested that Magellan named the passage Estrecho de Todos los Santos on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1520, and that Charles V afterwards attached Magellan's own name to it (Wikipedia, 'Strait of Magellan'). Corrected against research notes, which had read 1 November as the entry date: the entry was 21 October and the crossing ran thirty-eight days to 28 November. The First Narrows were passed in late October.
stops.campa: The channel closes to less than two miles at the First Narrows and then opens again, black water under black rock, glaciers standing over it, and at night fires burning on the southern shore, which the fleet names Tierra del Fuego for them. On All Saints' Day Magellan gives the whole passage the name Estrecho de Todos los Santos. It does not keep that name. Charles V afterwards orders it called after the man who found it, and Estrecho de Magallanes is the name on the charts from then on.
stops.quote: But the captain-general said that there was another strait for going out, and said that he knew it well, because he had seen it by a marine chart of the King of Portugal, which map had been made by a great pilot and mariner named Martin of Bohemia.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: The Martin Behaim chart Magellan is reported to have cited to his officers inside the strait
sources: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World

stops.name: The strait, the desertion of the San Antonio
stops.date_confidence: attested that the San Antonio deserted during the strait passage in November 1520 and reached Seville on 6 May 1521 with an account hostile to Magellan (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Strait of Magellan'). The precise day of the separation is given as about 20 November in the standard accounts. Same interior-channel pin as the preceding stop.
stops.campa: Deep in the channel Magellan sends the ships up separate arms to find which one goes through, and the San Antonio does not come back. Estêvão Gomes, her pilot, has put her captain in irons and turned her east for Spain, and she is the largest hull in the fleet and carries the greater part of what is left to eat. Magellan searches for her, plants a flag and a letter on a hill in case she returns, waits, and goes on with three ships on short rations. Gomes reaches Seville the following May with a story about a Portuguese who murdered Castilian officers and would not turn back.
suggested_refs: The Seville inquiry of May 1521 into the San Antonio's return and the testimony of Estêvão Gomes

stops.name: Cabo Deseado, out into the peaceful sea
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 28 November 1520 exit into the Pacific (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'; Wikipedia, 'Strait of Magellan'). Coordinates corrected: research notes gave -52.9309, -74.6963, roughly 24 km south of Cabo Pilar in open water. Cabo Pilar, the northwestern point of Desolación Island, lies at approximately 52°43'S 74°42'W, used here, and should be checked against a gazetteer before publication. Balboa had seen the Pacific from the Panamanian side in 1513; Indigenous navigators had crossed it for millennia.
stops.campa: Thirty-eight days after entering, the three ships come out past the last cape into open ocean, and Pigafetta says the captain general wept. He names the headland Cabo Deseado, the cape that was wanted. Ahead is water no European has crossed and none has measured, and Magellan reckons it a matter of weeks. It is the largest single thing on the surface of the earth. They will be on it three months and twenty days without sighting an inhabited shore, and the first stretch is so quiet that they name the whole ocean for the calm.
stops.quote: At the joy which the captain-general had at this he began to cry, and he gave the name of Cape of Desire to this cape, as a thing which had been much desired for a long time.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: Cabo Pilar and Cabo Deseado at the Pacific mouth of the strait, Desolación Island

stops.name: Umatac Bay, Guam, after ninety-eight days
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 6 March 1521 landfall on Guam, for roughly thirty deaths from starvation and scurvy in the crossing, and for the burning of houses and killing of islanders over stolen property (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). The Umatac Bay landing site is called traditionally cited rather than certain by Wikipedia, 'Humåtak'. The details of the diet are Pigafetta's.
stops.campa: By the end of it they are eating the ox hides off the yards, soaked in the sea for days and grilled, and sawdust, and rats at half a ducat apiece; the gums of the sick swell out over their teeth, and about thirty men die. On the sixth of March islands come up out of the water. Chamorro canoes come out fast under lateen sails and the islanders take what is not fastened down, including a ship's boat. Magellan lands a party, burns houses, kills seven men, and takes the boat back. He names the place the Islands of Thieves.
stops.quote: one of his principal virtues was constance in the most adverse fortune. In the midst of the sea he was able to endure hunger better than we.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: Umatac Bay, Guam, traditionally cited landing place of the fleet
sources: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World

stops.name: Homonhon, the watering place
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sighting of Samar on 16 March 1521 and the anchorage at Homonhon from 17 to 24 March, the island then uninhabited, with fishermen from Suluan making contact (Wikipedia, 'Homonhon Island'; Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan'). The tents for the sick and the trade goods are Pigafetta's detail.
stops.campa: They raise Samar on the sixteenth and anchor the next day off an uninhabited islet, where Magellan has two tents put up on the beach for the sick and a sow killed to feed them. On the eighteenth nine men come over from Suluan in a boat, and there is trade: fish, palm wine, bananas and coconuts against red caps, mirrors, small bells, combs. Pigafetta tastes palm wine for the first time and writes down the word for it. The crews rest eight days here. Magellan is calling this whole archipelago the islands of Saint Lazarus.
suggested_refs: Homonhon Island, first Philippine anchorage of the expedition, 17-24 March 1521

stops.name: Limasawa, the first Mass
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting with Rajah Kolambu and Rajah Siaui on 28 March and the Easter Sunday Mass by Father Pedro de Valderrama on 31 March 1521, with a cross planted on the island's high point (Wikipedia, 'Limasawa'). The identification of Pigafetta's Mazaua with Limasawa rather than a site near Butuan is the mainstream position and was the subject of long Philippine historical controversy, not re-litigated here.
stops.campa: At Limasawa the rajah Kolambu comes out in a boat, and Enrique of Malacca hails him, and the rajah understands what he says. Ten years after being carried west out of Malacca in another man's ownership, Enrique has arrived at a shore where his own speech is answered. On Easter Sunday Father Pedro de Valderrama says Mass on the beach with the two rajahs kneeling beside Magellan, and afterwards the men carry a cross up to the highest point of the island and set it where a ship at sea can see it.
suggested_refs: Limasawa (Mazaua) and the Philippine historiographical dispute over the site of the first Mass

stops.name: Cebu, the port and Rajah Humabon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival at Cebu and the meeting with Rajah Humabon on 7 April 1521 (Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'; Wikipedia, "Magellan's Cross"). The tribute refusal and the armour demonstration are Pigafetta's account. Coordinates are the exact Magellan's Cross site, 10°17'37"N 123°54'07"E, used as the Cebu harbour-side pin.
stops.campa: The three ships come into Cebu harbour on the seventh of April with their guns firing a salute, which frightens the town. Humabon rules the port and demands the tribute that every trading ship pays him. Magellan refuses to pay tribute on behalf of the king of Spain and offers an alliance instead. Then he has a demonstration put on for the town: a man in full plate is set upon by three swordsmen and takes no hurt from any of them. Humabon takes the alliance.
suggested_refs: Plaza Sugbo, Cebu City, and the port of Sugbu in 1521

stops.name: Cebu, the baptism and the Santo Niño
stops.date_confidence: attested for 14 April 1521 as the date of the baptism of Humabon and his consort as Carlos and Juana and of the gift of the image later venerated as the Santo Niño de Cebú (Wikipedia, 'Santo Niño de Cebú'; Wikipedia, 'Magellan expedition'). Research notes had collapsed this into the 7 April arrival and again into the 21 April cross-planting; both are corrected. The 1565 rediscovery is attested; the 44-year custody gap is real and undocumented, and continuity is devotional tradition, not record.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of April a platform is put up and Humabon is christened Carlos, for the emperor, and his consort Juana, for the emperor's mother. Some hundreds are baptised in the days that follow. To the queen Magellan gives a small carved image of the Christ Child. Forty-four years later, when Legazpi's men burn the coastal settlement, a Spanish mariner named Juan Camus is said to find that image whole in a pine box among the ashes, and Cebu has venerated it ever since. Where it was in the intervening years nothing records.
suggested_refs: The Santo Niño de Cebú and the Basílica Menor del Santo Niño, Cebu City

stops.name: Cebu, the cross on the shore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the planting of the cross on 21 April 1521 (Wikipedia, "Magellan's Cross"), for the tindalo casing of 1835 and the coral-stone pavilion of 1834, for the National Cultural Treasure declaration of 14 April 2021, and for the 2025 earthquake closure. Pigafetta's report that Magellan pressed converts to destroy their own religious objects is his own; the relic's physical continuity with 1521 is tradition rather than documented provenance.
stops.campa: A wooden cross is planted at the landing place on the twenty-first of April, a week after the baptisms, and Magellan tells the converts to burn their own images and keep the Christ Child in their place. Pigafetta, who likes these people and says so, sets the order down without comment. The cross outlasts everyone in the story. By 1835 devotees have been cutting slivers off it for their healing power and what is left is sheathed in tindalo wood, inside a coral-stone pavilion raised the year before. An earthquake closed the pavilion in 2025 and the candles go on burning outside the barrier.
suggested_refs: Magellan's Cross pavilion, Plaza Sugbo, National Cultural Treasure of the Philippines since 14 April 2021

stops.name: Mactan, the shallow water
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Battle of Mactan', citing Pigafetta: about sixty men, of whom forty-nine engaged and eleven stayed with the boats; the coral shallows holding the boats off; Magellan first struck by a poisoned arrow through his unarmoured legs, then speared in the arm and brought down by a kampilan. Research notes had omitted the poisoned arrow, which is Pigafetta's own detail and not a later accretion. Archival analysis cited in the research dossier holds that Magellan's royal instructions counselled avoiding unnecessary local conflict; that text was not fetched.
stops.campa: Lapulapu of Mactan will not acknowledge Humabon, or the king of Spain, or the tribute. Magellan goes over before dawn with sixty men, and the coral shoal reaches so far out that the boats ground a crossbow shot from the beach. Forty-nine of them wade in. Eleven stay with the boats and the ships' guns cannot reach that far. The Spanish shot glances off wooden shields; the islanders aim low, at the legs, which are not armoured. A poisoned arrow goes through his right leg, a spear takes him in the arm, and a kampilan brings him down in the shallows.
stops.quote: He, with a few of us, like a good knight, remained at his post without choosing to retreat further.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: The Mactan battle site and the Lapu-Lapu Shrine, Lapu-Lapu City
sources: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World

stops.name: Mactan, the body not given back
stops.date_confidence: attested that Lapulapu's side kept the bodies and refused Humabon's offer of merchandise in ransom, and that no account records what was done with them (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Mactan'). No grave has ever been identified. The 1866 Spanish-era obelisk, the 1969 national shrine declaration and the 1981 Lapulapu bronze are attested (Wikipedia, 'Mactan Shrine'). Coordinates are the Mactan Shrine complex.
stops.campa: Humabon sends to Lapulapu and offers merchandise, as much as they care to name, for the bodies of the captain general and the men who fell with him. Lapulapu refuses. He means to keep them. What was done with them afterwards nobody wrote down, and no grave has ever been found. The will signed in Seville twenty months before had asked for burial in a church of the Virgin near wherever he died, and there is no such church and no such burial. In 1866 the Spanish put an obelisk up on the shore; the bronze Lapulapu joins it in 1981.
stops.quote: the Indians threw themselves upon him, and ran him through with lances and scimetars, and all the other arms which they had, so that they deprived of life our mirror, light, comfort, and true guide.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: Mactan Shrine, Lapu-Lapu City: the 1866 Magellan obelisk and the 1981 Lapulapu statue on the same ground

stops.name: Cebu, the banquet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the killing of the expedition's surviving leaders, Duarte Barbosa and João Serrão among them, at Humabon's feast on 1 May 1521. Enrique's role is disputed in the sources and is not resolved here: Pigafetta has him survive the banquet, while Giovanni Battista Ramusio claimed he warned the chief that the Spaniards meant to seize the king. Research notes wrongly attributed that variant to Maximilianus Transylvanus; corrected. The banquet site itself is not independently located and the coordinates are the Cebu pin used above.
stops.campa: Four days after Mactan, Humabon invites the surviving officers ashore to receive the jewels he says he is sending to the king of Spain. Two dozen or more go, Duarte Barbosa and João Serrão among them, and they are killed at the table. Serrão is dragged bleeding to the water's edge and calls out to the ships to ransom him, and the ships cut their cables and stand out to sea and leave him on the beach. Enrique of Malacca, freed by a will nobody had read aloud to him, walks out of the European record at this point. Whether he had a hand in it is argued and cannot be settled.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Enrique of Malacca', for the Pigafetta and Ramusio versions of the banquet
sources: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World

stops.name: Tidore, the cloves he never saw
stops.date_confidence: posthumous: Magellan had been dead six and a half months and never reached this place. The stop is the fleet's, sailing under his commission, and is included as the geographic terminus of the enterprise he contracted for. The 8 November 1521 arrival at Tidore comes from the research dossier; the fetched Wikipedia article on Tidore confirms the island's sixteenth-century Spanish alliance but does not itself carry the date. The Moluccas arrival and the judgement that only Victoria was seaworthy for the return are attested (Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Magellan').
stops.campa: Six and a half months after his death the remaining ships come to anchor under the volcano at Tidore, and the sultan comes out to meet them, and the cloves are there, exactly where Francisco Serrão's letters had said they were. This is the place. The contract at Valladolid, the executions at San Julián, the thirty-eight days in the strait and the three months and twenty days on the Pacific were all aimed at this roadstead. Concepción has already been burned for want of men to sail her. Trinidad will not get home. Victoria loads clove until she is down to her marks.
suggested_refs: Tidore, Maluku, and the Spanish alliance with its sultanate against Portuguese Ternate
sources: Research dossier account of the 8 November 1521 arrival

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Victoria comes in
stops.date_confidence: posthumous, and not Magellan's own stop: the return belongs to Juan Sebastián Elcano and the surviving crew. Attested for the landfall at Sanlúcar on 6 September 1522 with eighteen European survivors (Wikipedia, 'Sanlúcar de Barrameda'; Wikipedia, 'Juan Sebastián Elcano'). Three Moluccans were also aboard, twenty-one in all reaching Seville. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Sanlúcar pin.
stops.campa: On the sixth of September a ship works in over the bar with her pumps going day and night and eighteen Europeans aboard, too weak to handle her without help from the shore. She is the Victoria. Juan Sebastián Elcano, who was one of the mutineers at San Julián and was pardoned for it, has brought her round the world the long way, down the Indian Ocean and round the Cape and up the Atlantic without touching a Portuguese port, on rice and water. Two hundred and seventy men went out in five ships. Eighteen come back in one.
stops.quote: he knew by his genius, and his intrepidity, without any one having given him the example, how to attempt the circuit of the globe, which he had almost completed.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Pigafetta, The First Voyage Round the World, trans. Lord Stanley of Alderley, Project Gutenberg #74723
suggested_refs: The Victoria's return to Sanlúcar de Barrameda, 6 September 1522

stops.name: Seville, the barefoot procession
stops.date_confidence: posthumous, and not Magellan's own stop. Attested that Victoria entered Seville on 8 September 1522 (Wikipedia, 'Juan Sebastián Elcano'). The penitential procession of the survivors is from the research dossier's general account and was not independently verified. Elcano's arms and the motto Primus circumdedisti me are standard and attested in the Elcano article. Coordinates are the Torre del Oro as a landmark proxy for the 1522 mooring, not a confirmed berth.
stops.campa: Two days later the Victoria comes up the river and moors at Seville, and the survivors go ashore barefoot, in shirts, carrying candles, to give thanks in the churches for having been brought back. They have been gone three years and twenty-eight days. Charles gives Elcano a coat of arms with a globe on it and the motto Primus circumdedisti me, you were the first to encircle me. The passage, the ocean and the strait carry Magellan's name in every atlas printed since. The arms granted for finishing the voyage do not mention him.
stops.quote: his conduct in the islands of Sebu and Matan, where he fell, defending the retreat of his companions, is more like that of the knights errant of an earlier date, than that of his contemporaries.
stops.quote_source: Lord Stanley of Alderley, editorial introduction to The First Voyage Round the World (Hakluyt Society, 1874); nineteenth-century editorial commentary, not primary testimony
suggested_refs: Elcano's grant of arms, 1523, with the globe and the motto Primus circumdedisti me
sources: Lord Stanley of Alderley, introduction to The First Voyage Round the World (1874)
